name: Arm Optimized Routines (string subproject)
baseline: the previous musl libc string routines in static aarch64 ClickHouse binaries (generic C and 2020-vintage Arm Optimized Routines assembly, per the PR description); glibc builds are not measured
workload: ClickHouse PR description: Arm's AdvSIMD/SVE/MTE string routines linked into ClickHouse for aarch64 and compared with the previous static-binary state, which used musl.
claimed_speedup: memcpy +26-37%, memmove ~2x on small sizes, memcmp +50-80%, strlen 2.9x, memchr 3x (vs the previous musl state, measured on Graviton4)
stars_or_usage: 716 stars; vendored by a pending ClickHouse PR
tradeoffs: Arm-specific assembly (string/aarch64, string/arm, some string/x86_64); MTE-aware variants exist. In the ClickHouse integration memcpy and memmove pick SVE or AdvSIMD at first call, the routines are linked with --whole-archive and libc is kept in sanitizer builds. Math routines from the same repo were reverted in that PR for 0.5-2.5 ULP error, so only the string routines are covered here.
caveats: The only numbers come from a ClickHouse pull request description (open and not merged as of 2026-10-11, opened 2026-09-08): no compiler, flags, benchmark tool or public harness stated, so tier C. The baseline is the previous musl routines (generic C plus 2020-vintage AOR assembly), so part of the gain is a newer version of the same Arm code; the PR description says glibc's aarch64 routines are already derived from AOR and that 'no large change in the perf suite is expected' on glibc builds, and gives no glibc numbers. The PR page also records a 12-17% regression on five ClickHouse queries on Graviton 3/4 in a glibc comparison (direction and cause not verified from the page). The repo's string/README.md gives no performance figures; string/bench holds benchmark code. A sibling search file may list this repo at tier D without these PR numbers.
found_via: WebSearch (github.com domains) 'faster than glibc memcpy strlen memchr strcmp optimized implementation' surfaced ClickHouse PR #118916; repo and PR opened on github.com

name: copies-and-fills (libcofi_rpi.so)
baseline: generic libc memcpy and memset on Raspberry Pi (ARM)
workload: Modified ssvb-membench with random numbers, iterating over sizes and source/destination alignments; memcpy and memset on a Raspberry Pi.
claimed_speedup: memcpy reaches performance parity with generic libc at around ~150 byte copies and 'eventually gains 2-3x throughput, especially when the source buffer is uncached' (up to 680 MB/s, effective 339 MB/s copy); memset reaches parity at around 100 bytes and peaks at 1390 MB/s, '~7x faster than the libc version'
hardware: Raspberry Pi (model and CPU not stated in the README; the notes mention a single-issue core)
tradeoffs: Hand-written ARM assembly (memcpy.s, memset.s) tuned for the original single-issue Raspberry Pi core; used by setting LD_PRELOAD=/full/path/to/libcofi_rpi.so. The misaligned-copy inner loop is derived from the GNU libc ARM port, hence LGPL. Not portable to other ARM cores or to 64-bit.
caveats: First-party claim in a 2012 README with no CPU model, compiler, flags, libc version or result tables; the benchmark harness is a modified copy of ssvb-membench that is not in this repo as far as the README says. The README says the library only reaches parity with libc at 100-150 bytes, so small copies gain nothing. The ~7x memset figure is a peak MB/s compared to libc, not a general average. Licence is stated as LGPL version 2.1 without 'or later'. Last commit 2012-08-03 and the hardware is obsolete.
found_via: Known LD_PRELOAD memcpy/memset replacement for Raspberry Pi; repo page and README opened on github.com after topic-page searches for memcpy/memset replacements

name: simstr
baseline: std::string and std::string_view idioms: concatenation, std::to_string, std::format hex formatting, find, replace and split code written with the C++ standard library
workload: Google Benchmark microbenchmarks (bench/bench_str.cpp) of string concatenation, number and hex formatting, literal search, replace-while-copying and split/parse, each against a plain std version of the same task.
claimed_speedup: Headline 'Speed up your work with strings by 2-10 times!'; per example: 1.6-2x concatenating with numbers, 9-14x hex formatting vs std::format, 1.5-9x literal concatenation and search in string_view, 1.5-2.2x conditional concatenation, 1.5x and higher replace-while-copying, 2-3x split and parse
compiler_and_flags: MSVC, Clang and GCC on Windows and Linux (WSL), plus an Emscripten WASM build; benchmark compiler versions and flags not stated (library tested with MSVC 19, Clang 19, GCC 13, Clang 21, Emscripten 4.0.6)
tradeoffs: Own string types and 'string expressions' API rather than a drop-in std::string; version 2.0.0 needs C++20 (concepts, std::format); the full library adds UTF conversion and shared/mutable string types.
caveats: Speedups are relative to the author's own 'before' std code in README examples, not an isolated std::string microbenchmark suite. Per-case results live on orefkov.github.io/simstr/results.html, which this session could not open (github.io blocked), so the ratios are taken from the README text and no CPU model is known. bench_str.cpp also pulls in StringZilla for comparison, which this run did not read. Which standard library (libstdc++, libc++, MSVC STL) backs each ratio is not stated.
found_via: vcpkg versions/baseline.json port list scan (orefkov-simstr), then github.com repo, README and bench/bench_str.cpp opened

name: ImGui SIMD ImStrlen/ImMemchr (PR #8421, Kraionix/ImGuiMemchrBench)
baseline: C standard library strlen and memchr (labelled CSTD in the PR; libc implementation and version not stated)
workload: Google Benchmark on std::string buffers of random ASCII from 1 MB to 1 GB: strlen scans for the terminator; memchr scans for 131-character lines ending in a newline; SSE, SSE+prefetch, AVX2 and AVX2+prefetch variants.
claimed_speedup: 1 GB buffer: ImStrlen AVX2_PREFETCH 56.6 ms (17.6 Gi/s) vs CSTD 79.9 ms (12.5 Gi/s); ImMemchr AVX2_PREFETCH 58.2 ms (17.17 Gi/s) vs CSTD 89.9 ms (10.93 Gi/s); PR title '55%'; a later comment says AVX2 ImMemchr gave 'about 60%' more performance on a 16 MB buffer and ImGui::TextUnformatted dropped from 1.6 ms to 0.98 ms per frame
compiler_and_flags: Compiler not stated; the bench repo only says 'Compiled benchmark in release'
hardware: Intel Core i9-10980XE (18 cores / 36 threads, all cores 4600 MHz, uncore 3200 MHz), 128 GB quad-channel at 4000 MHz, power saving disabled, AVX offset 400 MHz
stars_or_usage: 4 stars on the bench repo; proposed for Dear ImGui (PR open, not merged)
tradeoffs: x86-64 only (SSE and AVX2 variants; the bench repo's run_benchmark.ps1 exists 'to avoid crashes when avx512 is not supported'); the PR adds compile-time SIMD config macros (IMGUI_ENABLE_SSE, SSE4_2, AVX, AVX2). The maintainer rebased the PR and added ImStrlen/ImMemchr hooks (commit 1ec99f4, 2025-03-07) but the SIMD versions were not shown as merged; a reviewer argued libc should be optimized instead.
caveats: Numbers are from a PR thread; the bench repo README has no results table, no compiler or flags, and no LICENSE file (so reference only; the PR code would carry ImGui's licence if merged). Buffers of 1 MB to 1 GB are memory-bound and far from typical ImGui string lengths; the 60% figure is for one text-rendering workload. The run_benchmark.ps1 wrapper suggests Windows, so the CSTD baseline is probably the MSVC CRT rather than glibc (inference, not stated). Gains over glibc's own AVX2 strlen/memchr may be smaller.
found_via: WebSearch (github.com domains) 'faster than glibc memcpy strlen memchr strcmp optimized implementation' surfaced ocornut/imgui PR #8421; PR and Kraionix/ImGuiMemchrBench opened on github.com

name: optimization-detective (SWAR memcasecmp, common suffix and whitespace patches for Abseil)
baseline: Abseil absl::strings_internal::memcasecmp, FindLongestCommonSuffix and RemoveExtraAsciiWhitespace (verbatim upstream code from abseil-cpp@7e706921, byte-at-a-time loops)
workload: Standalone microbenchmarks (median of 25 reps, autotuned iteration count) of each function on 256 B to 4096 B strings: full match, half match, byte-identical and case-flipped equality.
claimed_speedup: FindLongestCommonSuffix 6.87x (full match 4096 B 1524 ns to 233 ns, 6.5x; 256 B 6.9x); memcasecmp 5.98x (eq_case 256 B 229 ns to 38 ns; 4096 B eq_exact 4.99x, eq_case 5.82x); RemoveExtraAsciiWhitespace 1.40x on already-clean input
tradeoffs: Header-only drop-in replacements (original.h, optimized.h, test.cc, bench.cc per function, no build system); the SWAR 8-byte loads assume little-endian and ASCII-only case folding; the suffix and case-compare versions pay about 0.5-1 ns extra when the mismatch is in the first or last byte.
caveats: Baseline is Abseil's scalar loop, not glibc strncasecmp or memcmp, so the ratios say nothing about libc (glibc uses SIMD for these on x86-64); only one machine (Apple M2) and one compiler. The repo's dollar and CO2 fleet estimates are heuristics, not evidence. Two more patches in the repo (nlohmann/json dump_escaped 4.62x, cpp-httplib header hash 1.44x) belong to JSON and HTTP categories and are not recorded here. Optimized code lives alongside verbatim Apache-2.0 Abseil source (original.h); the author's additions are MIT. Raw outputs under results/ were not opened (guessed file names returned 404); the tables are from FINDINGS.md. Tier A rests on public bench.cc, stated compiler, flags and CPU; a verifier should confirm the benchmark builds.
found_via: github.com/topics/swar listing (C++ entry 'drop-in performance patches for Abseil, nlohmann/json, and cpp-httplib'); repo README, FINDINGS.md and commits page opened
